claim: Mouse models of Rett syndrome display impaired excitatory neurotransmission.
source: Although mouse models of Rett syndrome (RTT), a postnatal neurological disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in MECP2, display impaired excitatory neurotransmission
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established finding from mouse models.

claim: The RTT phenotype can be largely reproduced in mice by removing MeCP2 from inhibitory GABAergic neurons.
source: the RTT phenotype can be largely reproduced in mice simply by removing MeCP2 from inhibitory GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citation to previous work (Chao et al., 2010) in the introduction.

claim: MeCP2 deficiency in glutamatergic neurons leads to early lethality.
source: MeCP2 deficiency in glutamatergic neurons leads to early lethality, obesity, tremor, altered anxiety-like behaviors, and impaired acoustic startle response
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by survival data showing CKO mice died by 10 weeks of age (Figure 3A).

claim: MeCP2 deficiency in glutamatergic neurons leads to obesity.

claim: MeCP2 deficiency in glutamatergic neurons leads to tremor.

claim: MeCP2 deficiency in glutamatergic neurons leads to altered anxiety-like behaviors.

claim: MeCP2 deficiency in glutamatergic neurons leads to impaired acoustic startle response.

claim: The phenotype of mice lacking MeCP2 only in glutamatergic neurons is distinct from the phenotype of mice lacking MeCP2 only in inhibitory neurons.
source: which is distinct from the phenotype of mice lacking MeCP2 only in inhibitory neurons.

claim: 98% of CamKII-positive glutamatergic neurons in the hippocampal CA1 region expressed Cre in Vglut2-Cre mice.

claim: Deleting or restoring MeCP2 only in glutamatergic neurons leads to complementary phenotypes of tremor, anxiety, and acoustic startle response.
source: it is surprising that deleting or restoring MeCP2 only in glutamatergic neurons leads to complementary phenotypes of tremor, anxiety, and acoustic startle response (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data summarized in Table 1.

claim: The caudal pontine reticular nucleus (PnC) is the major sensorimotor interface for acoustic startle response.
source: In the case of acoustic startle response, this is not entirely unexpected: the caudal pontine reticular nucleus (PnC) is the major sensorimotor interface, and proper glutamatergic signaling is necessary for the transmission of auditory information onto PnC neurons through action on AMPAR (Koch and Schnitzler, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: Proper glutamatergic signaling is necessary for the transmission of auditory information onto PnC neurons through action on AMPAR.
source: In the case of acoustic startle response, this is not entirely unexpected: the caudal pontine reticular nucleus (PnC) is the major sensorimotor interface, and proper glutamatergic signaling is necessary for the transmission of auditory information onto PnC neurons through action on AMPAR (Koch and Schnitzler, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: Restoring MeCP2 in neither excitatory nor inhibitory neurons alone is sufficient to fully rescue premature lethality.
source: Thus, restoring MeCP2 in neither excitatory nor inhibitory neurons alone is sufficient to fully rescue premature lethality.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the survival data in C-rescue mice and comparison with inhibitory rescue (Ure et al., 2016).

claim: Re-expressing MeCP2 in excitatory neurons failed to maintain body weight, as the C-rescue mice were underweight when compared with WT animals.
source: Similarly, re-expressing MeCP2 in excitatory neurons failed to maintain body weight, as the C-rescue mice were underweight when compared with WT animals, indicating the necessity of MeCP2 in inhibitory neurons to balance the circuit.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the weight data in C-rescue mice.

claim: The increased social interaction and repetitive behaviors observed in null mice were not induced in the CKO mice but were improved in the male C-rescue mice.
source: Interestingly, the increased social interaction and repetitive behaviors observed in null mice were not induced in the CKO mice but were improved in the male C-rescue mice.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the behavioral data.

claim: Restoring MeCP2 in glutamatergic neurons benefits stop-het females more than stop-null male mice.
source: One intriguing finding of this study is that restoring MeCP2 in glutamatergic neurons benefits stop-het females more than stop-null male mice: ataxia was normalized in the female, but not in the male, C-rescue mice.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data comparing male and female C-rescue mice.

claim: Female C-rescue mice retain MeCP2 in over 50% of non-glutamatergic neurons.
source: This is reasonable considering that in addition to the MeCP2 expressed in glutamatergic neurons, female C-rescue mice also retain MeCP2 in over 50% of non-glutamatergic neurons (Young and Zoghbi, 2004), none of which express MeCP2 at all in male C-rescue mice.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the difference between male and female C-rescue mice, with citation to supporting literature.

claim: Re-expressing MeCP2 only in GABAergic neurons is less effective in a heterozygous background than in the Mecp2-null background.
source: In this regard, it is interesting to note that re-expressing MeCP2 only in GABAergic neurons is less effective in a heterozygous background than in the Mecp2-null background (see companion paper Ure et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to the companion paper.

claim: It is easier for the brain to compensate for the loss of MeCP2 in 50% of inhibitory neurons than in 50% of excitatory neurons.
source: The opposite outcomes of these rescue strategies suggest that various types of neurons may be differentially sensitive to MeCP2 dosage, and it seems easier for the brain to compensate for the loss of MeCP2 in 50% of inhibitory neurons (glutamatergic female C-rescue) than in 50% of excitatory neurons (inhibitory female C-rescue).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the differential rescue outcomes.

claim: Deleting MeCP2 only in glutamatergic neurons resulted in reduced cortical activity in layer V pyramidal neurons of the somatosensory cortex.
source: At the circuit level, we demonstrated that deleting MeCP2 only in glutamatergic neurons resulted in reduced cortical activity in layer V pyramidal neurons of the somatosensory cortex, a defect also seen in the Mecp2-null mice.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the electrophysiology findings.

claim: MeCP2 plays an essential role in modulating the firing activity of excitatory neurons.
source: Together with the complete rescue of this defect by restoring MeCP2 only in glutamatergic neurons, this indicates an essential role of MeCP2 in modulating the firing activity of excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiology data in CKO and C-rescue mice.

claim: The dramatically reduced sEPSC charge reflects weakened excitatory drive onto the layer V neurons of CKO mice.
source: The dramatically reduced sEPSC charge reflects weakened excitatory drive onto the layer V neurons of CKO mice.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the electrophysiology data.

claim: The reduced firing activity in CKO mice may be region specific.
source: It is worth noting that this reduced firing activity in CKO mice may be region specific, as we also observed seizure-like spike-and-wave discharges in the cortex of these mice.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat to the interpretation of the reduced firing activity.

claim: Behavioral or electrographic seizures have been reported in Mecp2 whole brain inhibitory CKO mice.
source: Behavioral or electrographic seizures have also been reported in Mecp2 whole brain (Chao et al., 2010) and forebrain (Goffin et al., 2014) inhibitory CKO mice, as well as in somatostatin CKO mice (Ito-Ishida et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Seizures in Mecp2-null mice are caused by multi-level disruption of circuits that can arise from dysfunction of several different neuronal cell types.
source: These data suggest that the seizures we observe in Mecp2-null mice are caused by multi-level disruption of circuits that can arise from dysfunction of several different neuronal cell types.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the seizure data across different cell-type-specific models.

claim: Restoring MeCP2 only in excitatory neurons is insufficient to prevent seizure.
source: This is further supported by the C-rescue mice, as restoring MeCP2 only in excitatory neurons is insufficient to prevent seizure.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the seizure data in C-rescue mice.

claim: Postnatal loss of MeCP2 in forebrain excitatory neurons leads to motor coordination deficits, altered anxiety, and impaired social interaction.
source: Previous work has shown that postnatal loss of MeCP2 in forebrain excitatory neurons leads to motor coordination deficits, altered anxiety, and impaired social interaction (Gemelli et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: MeCP2 in glutamatergic neurons is important to prevent anxiety-like behaviors.
source: Through comparing and contrasting the excitatory conditional deletion and conditional rescue models, we confirmed the importance of MeCP2 in glutamatergic neurons to prevent anxiety-like behaviors.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: MeCP2 in glutamatergic neurons contributes to the pathogenesis of tremor.
source: Importantly, we also highlighted its contribution to the pathogenesis of tremor, which is a common and highly penetrant symptom in individuals with RTT (Klauck et al., 2002; Roze et al., 2007), and has not been reported in any other cell type-specific Mecp2 conditional deletion mouse.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the tremor data, with citations to supporting literature on RTT symptoms.

claim: Tremor is a common and highly penetrant symptom in individuals with RTT.
source: Importantly, we also highlighted its contribution to the pathogenesis of tremor, which is a common and highly penetrant symptom in individuals with RTT (Klauck et al., 2002; Roze et al., 2007)
evidence: This is stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: The autonomic dysfunction and premature death of Mecp2-null mice may be mainly driven by impaired excitatory signaling in the brainstem and spinal cord.
source: Expanding on the observations from Gemelli et al. and on previous studies on the autonomous dysfunction of RTT (Julu et al., 2001; Ward et al., 2011; Weese-Mayer et al., 2006), our work suggests that the autonomic dysfunction and premature death of Mecp2-null mice may be mainly driven by impaired excitatory signaling in the brainstem and spinal cord.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the data, with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Deficiency of MeCP2 in GABAergic neurons leads to ataxia, increased social interaction, repetitive behaviors, premature lethality, and obesity.
source: Our results precisely complement previous knowledge and work from Ure et al., which shows that deficiency of MeCP2 in GABAergic neurons leads to ataxia, increased social interaction, repetitive behaviors, premature lethality, and obesity
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings from the companion paper.

claim: Deficiency of MeCP2 in GABAergic neurons is less involved in tremor, altered anxiety, and impaired acoustic startle response.
source: but is less involved in tremor, altered anxiety, and impaired acoustic startle response.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings from the companion paper.

claim: This work provides an example of how primary deficits in excitatory signaling lead to neurological deficits.
source: This work also provides an example of how primary deficits in excitatory signaling lead to neurological deficits, which has ramifications for other postnatal neurological disorders, with disturbances in excitatory and inhibitory homeostasis, such as ASDs and intellectual disability.
evidence: This is stated as a broader implication of the findings.

claim: Vglut2 is the dominant glutamate vesicular transporter at embryonic and early postnatal stages.
source: Vglut2 is the dominant glutamate vesicular transporter at embryonic and early postnatal stages: by P14 it is mostly replaced by Vglut1 in the hippocampus, cortex, and cerebellum (Boulland et al., 2004; Fremeau et al., 2004; Miyazaki et al., 2003)
evidence: This is stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: By P14, Vglut2 is mostly replaced by Vglut1 in the hippocampus, cortex, and cerebellum.
source: Vglut2 is the dominant glutamate vesicular transporter at embryonic and early postnatal stages: by P14 it is mostly replaced by Vglut1 in the hippocampus, cortex, and cerebellum (Boulland et al., 2004; Fremeau et al., 2004; Miyazaki et al., 2003)
evidence: This is stated with citations to supporting literature.
